recurring_scale_anchors: 304×192 canvas; keep treatment scenes respectful, clear and non-graphic.
No readable words, letters, labels, brands or numbers; use marks and simple icons only.

Resolve vocabulary conflicts by the lesson group: operation is surgery, patient is a person receiving care, clinic is a care facility, medicine can mean the medical field, and tablet is a medication form.
Differentiate small adhesive strips from gauze wraps, cotton pads from loose cotton wool, medicine from medication, and urgent transport from outpatient care.
Use only mild first-aid scenes; no visible blood, invasive close-ups or alarming patient distress.

polysemy_resolution_table.ambulance: Emergency vehicle used to carry a patient to hospital; include a stretcher or medical cross, not a generic delivery van.
polysemy_resolution_table.clinic: A place that provides medical care; show a small outpatient clinic, not a clinical lecture.
polysemy_resolution_table.doctor: A medical professional examining or treating a patient.
polysemy_resolution_table.doctor's office: A small private practice with an exam room and doctor, not a general office desk.
polysemy_resolution_table.hospital: A large healthcare facility with treatment rooms and inpatient beds.
polysemy_resolution_table.nurse: A healthcare professional giving bedside care or checking a patient.
polysemy_resolution_table.paramedic: An emergency medical professional treating or transporting a patient in the field.
polysemy_resolution_table.patient (hospital): A person receiving medical care; use the hospital noun sense, not patient as an adjective.
polysemy_resolution_table.pharmacist: A trained professional preparing or dispensing medicine behind a pharmacy counter.
polysemy_resolution_table.pharmacy: A place where medicines are dispensed; include shelves and a pharmacist counter.
polysemy_resolution_table.waiting room: A clinic or hospital area where patients wait for appointments.
polysemy_resolution_table.appointment: A scheduled medical visit, implied by a patient and clinician meeting at a calendar or check-in desk; no readable writing.
polysemy_resolution_table.blood test: A small blood sample being collected into a test tube; keep it clean and non-graphic.
polysemy_resolution_table.injection: A clinician administering a simple injection with a syringe; avoid graphic needle detail.
polysemy_resolution_table.medical treatment: A clinician actively providing care, broader than one medicine or procedure.
polysemy_resolution_table.operation: A surgical procedure in an operating room, not the functioning of a machine.
polysemy_resolution_table.physical therapy / physiotherapy: A therapist guiding a patient through a controlled rehabilitation movement.
polysemy_resolution_table.prescription: A clinician providing a medicine order on a blank or mark-only sheet; no readable text or dosage.
polysemy_resolution_table.stitches: Sutures closing a small clean wound; show only a close, non-graphic skin detail.
polysemy_resolution_table.test results: A clinician and patient reviewing a simple chart with marks but no legible numbers or words.
polysemy_resolution_table.treatment: Care or therapy given for a condition; distinguish from the broad medical system and a single medication.
polysemy_resolution_table.vaccine: A vaccine vial and a clinician preparing a routine immunization.
polysemy_resolution_table.antiseptic: A topical liquid used to clean skin before first aid; distinguish from ordinary soap.
polysemy_resolution_table.antiseptic wipes: Individually wrapped cleaning wipes used on skin before treatment.
polysemy_resolution_table.inhaler: A handheld metered-dose medicine device, focused as an object rather than an asthma scene.
polysemy_resolution_table.medication / medicine (healthcare): Medicine taken to prevent or treat a health problem; use pills or a bottle, not the academic subject.
polysemy_resolution_table.medication: A drug or medicine used in care; draw a distinct medicine container or dose from the broader medical subject.
polysemy_resolution_table.medicine: The field of medical science and care, as distinct from a particular medication.
polysemy_resolution_table.ointment: A small tube or jar of topical medicated cream applied to skin.
polysemy_resolution_table.painkillers: Pain-relieving medicines as a group, shown as several tablets or capsules with no labels.
polysemy_resolution_table.pain reliever: A single medicine that reduces pain; show one clear dose or bottle, distinct from the plural category.
polysemy_resolution_table.pill / pills (tablets): Solid oral medicine tablets or capsules, not an electronic tablet.
polysemy_resolution_table.tablet: A single flat solid medicine dose in the healthcare sense, not a digital device.
polysemy_resolution_table.dose: One measured amount of medicine at a time, shown with a spoon or single marked cup but no readable numbers.
polysemy_resolution_table.side effect: An unintended mild effect after medicine, such as drowsiness; distinguish from an allergy rash.
polysemy_resolution_table.allergy: An immune reaction to a trigger such as pollen or an animal; show a mild reaction without labeling.
polysemy_resolution_table.adhesive bandage: A small adhesive strip placed over a minor cut; distinguish from a gauze wrap.
polysemy_resolution_table.adhesive tape: Medical tape securing gauze to skin, not office or packing tape.
polysemy_resolution_table.bandage: A gauze wrap supporting or covering an injured area; distinguish from a small adhesive strip.
polysemy_resolution_table.cotton pads: Flat, round absorbent pads used for cleaning or applying medicine.
polysemy_resolution_table.cotton wool: Loose, fluffy absorbent cotton used in first aid; not cotton fabric or a cotton plant.
polysemy_resolution_table.first aid kit: A compact box containing simple supplies such as gauze, tape and scissors.
polysemy_resolution_table.safety pin: A clasping pin used to secure a bandage or sling; keep the point covered.
polysemy_resolution_table.scales (measure): A personal weighing scale used to check body weight, not luggage or a map scale.
polysemy_resolution_table.scissors: Small blunt-ended medical scissors used to trim gauze or tape, not kitchen or office cutting.
polysemy_resolution_table.stethoscope: A flexible listening instrument with chest piece and earpieces used by a clinician.
polysemy_resolution_table.syringe: A calibrated medical syringe without readable numbers; do not confuse it with the needle alone.
polysemy_resolution_table.thermometer: A clinical thermometer measuring body temperature, with no readable numbers.
polysemy_resolution_table.tweezers: A small paired-tip first-aid tool for grasping a splinter; draw the tool clearly.
polysemy_resolution_table.drink water: A patient drinking water during recovery; use a clear glass or bottle.
polysemy_resolution_table.exercise: Gentle, regular movement as part of health and recovery, not intense gym training.
polysemy_resolution_table.feel better: A clear improvement in comfort after rest or care, shown by relieved expression and upright posture.
polysemy_resolution_table.gain weight: A neutral, nonjudgmental increase in body weight; imply it with a scale and an upward trend, no numbers.
polysemy_resolution_table.heal: A wound or injury gradually closing; show a clean healing process without graphic detail.
polysemy_resolution_table.lie down: A person moving into or resting in a horizontal position for care.
polysemy_resolution_table.lose weight: A neutral, nonjudgmental decrease in body weight; imply it with a scale and a downward trend, no numbers.
polysemy_resolution_table.recover: A gradual return of strength after illness, distinct from one moment of feeling better.
polysemy_resolution_table.rest: A quiet pause that supports health; distinguish from being unable to sleep.
polysemy_resolution_table.resuscitate: A trained responder performing CPR on a practice manikin or fully clothed patient; non-graphic and respectful.

glossary_context_notes: Use the group title to override inaccurate Japanese glosses when the listed term is clearly a healthcare word.

“Medication / medicine (healthcare)” and “medication” both normalize to the medication slug; name their source files medication-healthcare.svg and medication.svg.
When illustrating dose or syringe, omit readable measurements.
No medical card should imply guaranteed weight loss or weight gain; keep both concepts neutral.
